headers: Book case, design lesson and its use
Feedback and making it easy to join
rows:
01 · Ask About a Detail

Choose part of an object image. Say what you notice. Ask AI one question, then say what you think after its answer.

Possible concept evidence: the chosen detail, question, actual answer and any change in the visitor’s explanation.

After an AI answer, what does a visitor use to decide what to believe about an object?

We look for reasons, such as a visible detail, a museum source or personal knowledge. We also ask when the person checks or rejects the answer.

A connection to an object can come from its history, appearance or a personal memory. These are different reasons. We keep them separate when reading the visitor’s account. This uses relational authenticity and the difference between looking alike and having a real source link. [1] [2]

The 9 October interview participant found this fairly ordinary. It has a low entry burden, but a blank question box can still be hard to use. Offer a few details to choose from and allow a short spoken question. A person can use the source card without AI.

Keep as an introduction.

Museum AI questions can help visitors begin A or B. A separate study could focus on how the order of explanations shapes their understanding.

Basis: heritage-agent attitudes and Cleveland’s Talk to the Art. [13] [23]

02 · Make with AI on My Cuff or Bag

Selected as A. Look at a textile, assemble ordinary materials, photograph the arrangement and let AI combine both inputs. Rearrange, photograph again and compare the next response. A cuff or bag is the digital output setting.

Round 1: actual arrangement and comparison with prepared examples selected manually. See the separate round plan.

How do people maintain or revise their understandings of authenticity through interaction with AI and cultural heritage?

The cuff or bag is an interaction form. The research concerns what people understand as authentic, and how that understanding develops through the encounter.

Relational authenticity helps us ask how the visitor connects a new result to the source work. Looking similar, knowing the maker’s history and having made something yourself are separate grounds. Follow the grounds the visitor introduces. [1] [2]

The 2 October meeting linked Probe 2 to authenticity and clothing. The 9 October interview suggested a take-away and choice about AI. Ordinary materials, large pieces, pointing and assistance support participation. The arrangement is the core input, with cuff or bag imagery as a presentation choice.

Develop as A.

Art Morph supplies a close material-and-AI precedent. Our study follows how source-related reasons develop when visitors guide a pattern onto a personal item through two local actions.

Basis: Art Morph, embodied generation, Huayao making and ZOMA. [22] [29] [30] [12] [7]

03 · Change One Detail

Select an area of an image, tell AI what may change, then compare the changed version with the source.

Possible concept evidence: selected area, instruction, actual image and reasons for keeping or rejecting it.

Which changes still feel connected to the object, and which changes lose that connection?

We need to hear why a change matters. Ask what the preferred picture carries from the source. The HCI issue is how people set and check limits for generation.
The difference between resemblance and a real source link helps us separate “looks like it” from “still carries something important from it”. We also record personal preference on its own. [2] [5]

The 9 October interview questioned the purpose of changing an image. The 2 October meeting’s clothing idea supplies a possible use. The current A brings that use into a two-round material interaction.

Pause as a separate probe.

New A now includes two visual responses guided by material action. Keep Probe 3 only if a clear different use emerges, such as adapting a particular detail to clothing.

Basis: TwistLens, Gen-Diaolou and Cleveland’s Extend the Art show that image transformation already has precedents. [5] [14] [24]

04 · Write a Label Together

Selected together with 5 as B. Original interpretations, AI language/image assistance, real replies and clarification form an exchange. A related postcard carries its outcome.

Round 1: original-language messages and replies stay visible, with postcards made from selected messages and prepared images.

Full B options: a digital interface or paper conversation board with AI assistance. A printed postcard can be explored later.

How do people express and negotiate their understanding of a shared heritage object through AI-mediated cross-cultural exchange?

Follow what a person expresses, what another person understands and how they clarify or retain different interpretations.

Authentication means a process through which an account comes to be accepted. We ask who accepts a museum explanation and on what grounds. Research on AI writing also helps us check whether a person still recognises their voice. [17] [3]

The 2 October meeting connected 4 and 5 with multilingual exchange. The 9 October interview saw overlap between them. A shared postcard lets a person reply to an earlier visitor, while the source, crop and card stay linked.

Combine with 5 as B.

The card develops through a real reply and clarification. The final version is the record people can keep.

Basis: language control, cultural detail and museum AI text. [8] [9] [25]

05 · Share a Detail

Combined with 4 as B. A source-related meaning is shared, answered and clarified. The conversation remains visible, with a connected postcard people can keep.

Round 1: the message area and postcard area share one local whiteboard.

How does a personal meaning develop when another visitor responds to the postcard?

We compare what the sender meant, what the recipient understood and what the sender clarifies. Words and the pattern preview are part of the same exchange.

Relational authenticity helps us follow how the object connects people. Personal voice helps us ask whether the author recognises the description. We keep historical accuracy, translation, understanding and image approval separate. [1] [3] [16]

The 9 October feedback suggested merging 4 and 5 and giving people a take-away. The concept keeps exchange and its postcard connected. Round 1 offers own-card paper copies, with no contact collection.

Combine with 4 as B.

The interaction centres on cross-cultural expression and response. The postcard carries a chosen message from that interaction. Round 1 is the first low-fidelity exploration of this direction.

GIFT and museum data souvenirs provide precedents. [15] [26]
